WFP Burkina 
May 2026 
Contact info: Liam Wylie (liam.wylie@wfp.org) 
Country Director: ai Aline SAMU (aline.samu@wfp.org) 
 
WFP BURKINA FASO 
COUNTRY BRIEF 
May 2026 
KEY HIGHLIGHTS 
• In April, WFP assisted 415,351 people, delivering 
3,590 mt of food. This reflects a slight decrease 
compared to March, mainly due to operational 
constraints, while efforts continued to reach 
vulnerable populations. 
• Humanitarian needs remain significant, 
underscoring the importance of sustained 
assistance to protect vulnerable populations and 
consolidate recent gains. 
• WFP continues an integrated response across 
food assistance, nutrition, school meals and 
resilience, requiring USD 99.6 million for May–
October 2026 to sustain operations and avoid 
further deterioration in food security.

Photo Caption & Credit: WFP/Photographer Jecuthiel Yameogo 
 
SITUATION OVERVIEW 
 
• Burkina Faso faces a complex crisis driven by 
insecurity, climate shocks, and structural 
vulnerabilities. Reliance on rainfed agriculture 
heightens exposure to climate variability. Insecurity 
remains the primary driver of humanitarian needs, 
with 2 million internally displaced persons (latest 
official figure, March 2023), limiting access to land, 
markets, and essential services. 
• The preliminary results from the April 2026 national 
food security and nutrition analysis projects 1.66 
million people will face crisis-level food insecurity (IPC 
Phase 3+), including 223,000 people in emergency 
situations, during the June–August 2026 lean season, 
compared to 2.3 million in 2025. While the situation 
shows an overall improvement relative to last year, 
access constraints remain significant in several 
regions, despite localized progress observed in 2025 
such as the restoration of access to Titao and 
Barsalogho. 
• Already in 2025, funding shortfalls forced WFP to 
reduce its coverage by around 30 percent compared 
to 2024, contributing to deteriorating food 
consumption and increased negative coping 
strategies among vulnerable households. WFP 
continues to deliver an integrated response including 
emergency food and nutrition assistance, school 
feeding, resilience activities, and common services 
through UNHAS, supporting national efforts toward 
stabilization and food sovereignty.
WFP Burkina Faso Country Brief 
May 2026 
OPERATIONAL UPDATES 
General Food Assistance 
• In April, WFP distributed over 2,907 mt of food and 
nutrition assistance to 197,404 people in localities 
such as Silmague, Seguenega, and Diapaga, 
including 180 mt airlifted to localities such as 
Kantchari or Gorgadji. 
• WFP took part in two government-mandated 
convoys: one to Gayeri and another to Sebba and 
Solhan. WFP had last joined convoys to these 
locations in April 2025 and December 2024, 
respectively. 
• The main challenge remains funding constraints, 
which limit WFP’s ability to meet needs. In addition, 
two WFP airlift helicopters were unavailable due to 
operational and administrative constraints, 
significantly reducing airlift capacity and increasing 
reliance on road transport. 
Nutrition 
• WFP supported malnutrition prevention by 
assisting 855 young children and 553 women, while 
screening over 2,600 children and identifying very 
few cases of moderate malnutrition; nutrition 
awareness reached more than 4,300 people. 
• To treat moderate acute malnutrition, WFP 
provided specialized nutritious foods to over 
31,700 children and 15,600 women. 
• WFP also strengthened local production of fortified 
foods through quality audits and training for 
national producers, improving standards and 
capacity. 
School-Based Assistance 
• In April, WFP reached 236,644 students (56 percent 
girls) with daily hot meals in 755 schools, including 
7,259 students who received take-home rations 
(THR), to support attendance and retention. 
• Under the integrated programme, 171,950 
students (56 percent girls) in 629 schools received 
hot meals, with THR provided to upper primary 
students meeting attendance criteria. Under 
emergency school feeding, 64,694 students (54 
percent girls) in 126 schools were assisted, 
including 34,484 IDPs, with support limited to on-
site meals due to funding constraints. 
• Efforts focused on programme quality and capacity 
strengthening (field monitoring, partnerships, 
kitchen construction), alongside coordination with 
partners and government, including Education 
Cluster engagement and planning for the phase-
out of emergency school feeding by end-2026. 
Resilience and Livelihood Support 
• In April 2026, WFP strengthened community 
resilience through the Food Assistance for Assets 
(FFA) programme, supporting the production of 
185 compost heaps (9 m³ each), treatment of 17 
gullies, and restoration of 86 hectares of degraded 
land. Activities also included the construction of 
2,101 improved cookstoves, rehabilitation of 14 
water ponds, seedling production, and assistance 
to 2,686 beneficiaries with 266 mt of food. 
• Through the Smallholder Agricultural Market 
Support (SAMS) programme, WFP reinforced 
livelihoods by supporting farmer organization 
targeting and delivering SBCC messaging, while 
strengthening capacities through trainings of 40 
participants (13 women) on GBV/PSEA and data 
collection, alongside project staff induction and 
technical workshops. 
United Nations Humanitarian Air Service 
(UNHAS) 
• In April 2026, UNHAS supported humanitarian 
operations through 246 flights to 27 destinations, 
serving 71 user organizations, and transporting 
1,351 passengers as well as 22.9 mt of light cargo. 
Despite limited flight cancellations, UNHAS 
maintained access to isolated and hard-to-reach 
locations, including Bourzanga, Gorgadji, Arbinda, 
Djibo, and other remote areas. 
 
FUNDING OVERVIEW 
Country Strategic Plan (2019-2026) 
 
 
Donors: 
Donors to WFP’s Burkina Faso Country Strategic Plan include 
Austria, Burkina Faso, Canada, Denmark, the European 
Commission, Finland, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, 
Luxembourg, Monaco, the Netherlands, Norway, the Republic 
of Korea, the Russian Federation, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, 
the United Kingdom and the United States of America. 
Additional support was provided by the UN Central Emergency 
Response Fund (CERF) and private donors, including the Ajram 
Foundation, Buddhist Global Relief, the Gwendolyn Sexton 
Foundation, and The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day 
Saints.

related.excerpt: NEW TAIPEI CITY, Taiwan — China’s newest air-to-air missile, the PL-16, could vie with an equivalent advance by the U.S. military and give the People’s Liberation Army an edge in any Asia-Pacific conflicts because of its increased travel distance and a second-wind feature, experts say. The PL-16 beyond-visual-range missile as described in social and trade media would answer Lockheed Martin’s AIM-260 Joint Advanced Tactical Missile (JATM) for the U.S. armed forces, analysts believe, and improve on previous generations developed in China. They say China’s missile boasts a long total flight distance estimated at 200 to 300 kilometers (124 to 186 miles) and dual-pulse or variable-thrust rocket motor technology that allow for a second burst of propulsion late in flight, the Indian defense news portal Indian Defence Research Wing said in a June 3 analysis. Lockheed Martin’s system is also expected to feature extra propulsion for flights beyond visual range and travel at least 200 kilometers. The PL-16’s specs would let it chase large, slower-moving aircraft, said Malcolm Davis, a senior analyst for defense strategy and national security with the Australian Strategic Policy Institute. related.title: Ukraine launches ‘TrophyLab’ platform to share captured Russian weapons with allies
related.summary: VIENNA — Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense launched an access-controlled online platform last week that provides allied governments, defense companies and research institutions with technical intelligence drawn from captured Russian military hardware − a formalization of what Kyiv has long done informally with select partners.
bullets: VIENNA — Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense launched an access-controlled online platform last week that provides allied governments, defense companies and research institutions with technical intelligence drawn from captured Russian military hardware − a formalization of what Kyiv has long done informally with select partners.

Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov announced the launch on social media Thursday, framing the platform as a strategic tool for “the entire civilized world.” Among the listed items available for study are, for example, a Kinzhal hypersonic missile and a T-90M tank.

Among similar moves, Ukraine has previously shared countless hours of frontline drone footage to train allied AI systems and signed a bilateral agreement with Germany − the so-called Brave Germany program − to jointly support startups to develop deep-strike weapons based on lessons learned in the field.

Beyond digital access, the platform allows verified partners to request the physical hardware itself for non-destructive inspection, disassembly or full destruction testing, a provision that could prove particularly valuable for nations developing electronic countermeasures or seeking to harden their own platforms against specific Russian threats.
The initiative fits into a broader pattern of Kyiv institutionalizing battlefield knowledge as a transferable asset.
related.excerpt: VIENNA — Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense launched an access-controlled online platform last week that provides allied governments, defense companies and research institutions with technical intelligence drawn from captured Russian military hardware − a formalization of what Kyiv has long done informally with select partners. The snazzily branded platform, called TrophyLab and accessible at trophylab.mod.gov.ua, currently catalogs more than 115 samples of seized Russian equipment across 79 categories. Users who pass a vetting process gain access to blueprints, component analyses, schematics, and the findings of Ukrainian state laboratories and intelligence agencies − more than 225 studies at present, according to the ministry. related.summary: Mediators Qatar and Pakistan said Washington and Tehran agreed to a roadmap towards ⁠a final deal within 60 days and that technical talks ​would continue for the rest of the week in the Swiss mountain resort of Buergenstock. US-Iran talks set to continue despite Iranian walkout The first round of face-to-face talks between the US and Iran ended in Switzerland on Monday, mediators said, after a tense opening marked by Tehran saying it had again closed the strait of Hormuz and Donald Trump repeating his threats to resume attacks on Iran.
bullets: Mediators Qatar and Pakistan said Washington and Tehran agreed to a roadmap towards ⁠a final deal within 60 days and that technical talks ​would continue for the rest of the week in the Swiss mountain resort of Buergenstock.

US-Iran talks set to continue despite Iranian walkout The first round of face-to-face talks between the US and Iran ended in Switzerland on Monday, mediators said, after a tense opening marked by Tehran saying it had again closed the strait of Hormuz and Donald Trump repeating his threats to resume attacks on Iran.

The parties agreed to a mechanism to end Israel’s war in Lebanon and opened a communications line to help ensure safe passages for commercial ships through the Hormuz strait, ⁠ according to the joint statement which said that the first session of talks under the US-Iran agreement had concluded.

Photograph: Getty Images Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said on social media his country had secured waivers for oil and petrochemical ⁠exports, the release of some frozen assets and the launch of a reconstruction and development plan for Iran.

Iran said at the weekend that it had again stopped maritime traffic through the ​Hormuz strait, in response to continuing fighting in Lebanon between Hezbollah and Israel, and that Sunday’s talks would not cover substantive issues such as Iran’s nuclear program.
